{"schema_version":"1.0","handoff_id":"handoff_42q35uni5ktu","explanation_id":"expl_8k7oi6xzxt19","round":"first","quiz":{"questions":[{"position":1,"concept_id":"c_amphipathic_phospholipids","prompt":"In a phospholipid bilayer, which part of each phospholipid faces the water on both sides?","options":{"a":"The water-avoiding tails","b":"The water-loving heads","c":"The cholesterol molecules","d":"The sugar chains on the outer surface"}},{"position":2,"concept_id":"c_fatty_acid_saturation","prompt":"Why do double bonds in unsaturated fatty acid tails increase membrane fluidity?","options":{"a":"They attach sugars to the tails","b":"They make the tails pack more tightly together","c":"They kink the tails, hindering close packing","d":"They bind cholesterol to the tails"}},{"position":3,"concept_id":"c_fatty_acid_saturation","prompt":"Compared with saturated fatty acid tails, unsaturated tails in a membrane tend to:","options":{"a":"Pack less closely and allow more movement","b":"Pack closely and reduce movement","c":"Form the glycocalyx","d":"Prevent lipids from moving between leaflets"}},{"position":4,"concept_id":"c_fluidity_factors","prompt":"Which of the following affects membrane fluidity?","options":{"a":"The number of sugars on the outer surface","b":"Whether proteins are present in the membrane","c":"Which leaflet a lipid sits in","d":"The chain length of the fatty acid tails"}},{"position":5,"concept_id":"c_cholesterol_buffer","prompt":"In a very fluid membrane, what does cholesterol do?","options":{"a":"Increases fluidity further","b":"Restrains movement and limits excessive fluidity","c":"Converts unsaturated tails to saturated tails","d":"Moves lipids to the other leaflet"}},{"position":6,"concept_id":"c_cholesterol_buffer","prompt":"In cold conditions, how does cholesterol help the membrane?","options":{"a":"It prevents excessive stiffening","b":"It makes the membrane freeze solid","c":"It adds double bonds to the tails","d":"It hides the heads from water"}},{"position":7,"concept_id":"c_fluid_mosaic_model","prompt":"What does the fluid mosaic model describe?","options":{"a":"A membrane of phospholipids with fixed proteins","b":"Two leaflets with identical composition","c":"A mixture of lipids, cholesterol, and proteins whose components can move sideways","d":"A sugar wall outside the cell"}},{"position":8,"concept_id":"c_membrane_asymmetry","prompt":"Which statement about lipid movement between membrane leaflets is supported by the explanation?","options":{"a":"Lipids switch leaflets freely without any help","b":"Lipids rarely switch leaflets without enzymes such as flippases","c":"Flippases move cholesterol into the glycocalyx","d":"The two leaflets always have identical composition"}},{"position":9,"concept_id":"c_glycocalyx_recognition","prompt":"What is the glycocalyx?","options":{"a":"Sugars on the outer membrane surface that help cells recognize one another","b":"The inner layer of water-avoiding tails","c":"A type of cholesterol molecule","d":"An enzyme that flips lipids between leaflets"}},{"position":10,"concept_id":"c_glycocalyx_recognition","prompt":"Which role is supported for the glycocalyx?","options":{"a":"Setting the composition of each leaflet","b":"Restraining fluid movement in the cold","c":"Lowering the chain length of fatty acid tails","d":"Distinguishing self from non-self"}}]},"answer_key":[{"position":1,"correct_option":"b","rationale":"Phospholipid heads are water-loving and face water on both sides, while the water-avoiding tails are tucked inside the bilayer."},{"position":2,"correct_option":"c","rationale":"Double bonds kink unsaturated tails, making close packing harder and increasing membrane fluidity."},{"position":3,"correct_option":"a","rationale":"Saturated tails pack closely, while kinked unsaturated tails pack less closely, allowing more movement and higher fluidity."},{"position":4,"correct_option":"d","rationale":"The explanation lists tail saturation, chain length, temperature, and cholesterol as factors affecting membrane fluidity."},{"position":5,"correct_option":"b","rationale":"Cholesterol restrains movement when the membrane is very fluid, buffering fluidity rather than increasing it."},{"position":6,"correct_option":"a","rationale":"Cholesterol prevents excessive stiffening of the membrane in the cold, which is part of its buffering role."},{"position":7,"correct_option":"c","rationale":"The fluid mosaic model describes a mixture of lipids, cholesterol, and proteins whose components can move sideways."},{"position":8,"correct_option":"b","rationale":"The explanation says lipids rarely switch leaflets without enzymes such as flippases, floppases, and scramblases."},{"position":9,"correct_option":"a","rationale":"The glycocalyx is formed by sugars on the outer surface and helps cells recognize one another."},{"position":10,"correct_option":"d","rationale":"The explanation says the glycocalyx helps cells recognize one another, including distinguishing self from non-self."}]}
